# Story & scripts

## Script

### Hook, problem, journey, lesson, CTA
<a id="story-hook-problem-journey-lesson-cta"></a>

Caleb's flexible story frame: hook, specific relatable stakes, the journey with its low points and messy middle (progress, not perfection), a usable lesson in chunked steps, then a call to action. Rules can be broken.

> You now have the rules. Feel free to break the rules.

`script` · formats: reel30, reel60, reel90, yt-short, yt-long · niches: all · stated · from [L05](../sources/L05.md)

### Story types: origin, failure, success, client
<a id="story-origin-retell"></a>

Origin stories resonate most, so keep retelling them (every post meets a cold audience). Failure stories with the lesson build trust (losses are more relatable than wins; don't be a robot). Success, before/after and client wins are the proof.

> You need to treat your content like you're always trying to reach a cold audience

`script` · formats: reel30, reel60, reel90, yt-short, yt-long, carousel · niches: all · stated · from [L05](../sources/L05.md)

Related: [Stories sell twice a week, nurture the rest](../topics/growth.md#growth-stories-nurture-sell)

### Industry trope, then your contrary view
<a id="story-industry-contrarian"></a>

State the industry trope, then your contrary belief, respectfully and without naming names ("never tell your audience about your offer in your organic content").

> never tell your audience about your offer in your organic content

### Script: hook → story → 2 points
<a id="story-hook-story-two-points"></a>

Hook ("Kick Coffee is the best coffee shop in Newport Beach"), a real anecdote, then your two reasons.

### "8 Mile": disprove the counter-argument first
<a id="story-8-mile"></a>

After the hook, call out the opposite argument and disprove it, then make your point; it removes objections up front and keeps people watching.

> call out the opposite argument and disprove it

`script` · formats: reel60, reel90, yt-short, yt-long · niches: all · stated · from [L06](../sources/L06.md)

### 4 or 5 mini takes
<a id="story-4-5-things"></a>

"Observations I made at Coachella as a brand strategist": 4–5 mini videos in one, each a strong take; people stay for the next one.

### Conflict and a shared enemy
<a id="story-conflict-everywhere"></a>

Build every example on conflict: before/after, problem/solution, an enemy (A = approach, B = belief, C = competitor), juxtaposition. Tristan: a shared enemy is one of the best copywriting principles.

> We as human beings… remember stuff relatively

`script` · formats: reel30, reel60, reel90, yt-short, yt-long, carousel, story, podcast · niches: all · stated · from [L09](../sources/L09.md), [L08](../sources/L08.md)

Related: [Who, what to say, how to say it](../topics/process.md#proc-who-say-how)

### Hinge stories on "but"
<a id="story-conflict-via-but"></a>

Tell a story around the word "but" without writing it: what went wrong next (woke 8:52, mum blocks the door over blue shorts…) instead of "I got on the train, had a coffee".

> You just go but but but. What went wrong? That's… conflict.

### Intro = time, place, what's happening
<a id="story-time-place-intro"></a>

Open with the time, the place and what is going on in your life right now (the "3:47 a.m." intro); noticing what is in front of you is the material and should feel "warm to touch".

### Open loops, re-open one at ~15 s
<a id="story-open-loops"></a>

Open curiosity at the start and keep opening loops with illustrations, metaphors and stats. Viewers who got the point 15 s in leave, so re-open a new loop around 15 s; a spoken "Why?" works. Caleb wants editors who "open and close loops".

> open and close loops to retain attention

`script` · formats: reel30, reel60, reel90, yt-short, yt-long · niches: all · stated · from [L08](../sources/L08.md), [L05](../sources/L05.md)

### Statement, reason, re-hook, "Why?", payoff
<a id="story-live-hook-build"></a>

Briar's live script: strong statement, a one-sentence reason (so people aren't annoyed), a stronger re-hook with high stakes, "Why?" to open the next loop, the payoff, then a wild closing line as a comment driver.

### Outlines and mechanisms: blitz, storytime, opinions
<a id="story-controversial-outline"></a>

Simple outline Oren uses all the time: controversial question → rapid-fire opinions → justifications → punchline. Reliable mechanisms: "blitz" rapid-fire lists ("10 out of 10 niche habits…") and storytime.

> It's a controversial question, rapid fire opinions, justifications, punch line.

### Structure = dividing lines + parallelism
<a id="story-dividing-lines-parallelism"></a>

Split the piece into clear parts with matching headings (first 100 readers / next 9,900) so it's cohesive. David adds the 1971 paper "That's Interesting": show two things thought different are one, or one thing is two.

> Structuring is just dividing lines and parallelism.

<a id="story-honest-limitation"></a>

### Answer objections inside the content
<a id="story-answer-objections"></a>

Mine comments (and sales calls) for recurring objections and answer them in future content, like a video sales letter; Oren summarises call objections weekly and feeds them back into content.

## Edit

### Long form: spread the value, don't front-load
<a id="story-yt-long-spread-value"></a>

A YouTube editor builds tension, stakes and open loops and spreads value through the video instead of front-loading it all in the first 3 minutes (watch time).

> YouTube loves watch time
